Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Reading the Poem Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.2): answer questions on joining hands and helping each other.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud with expression, pausing after each couplet to let students absorb the imagery of joined hands and shared cheering. Students follow along in their textbooks (pp.1–2).

Choral reading: the class reads the poem together twice, the teacher modelling rhythmic stress on the end rhymes (tall/fall, sing/anything). Students tap the desk lightly on each rhyming word to feel the poem's beat.

Let us Think — A. (p.2): teacher reads each question aloud, students discuss briefly in pairs, then share answers with the class. Teacher writes key phrases on the board ('the goal is near', 'bond of trust').

Quick close: students say one word that describes the feeling of the poem's closing couplet ('Together we shine, our hearts as one'). Teacher collects two or three responses to gauge first impressions.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's end-rhyme scheme (tall/fall, sing/anything, share/there, near/cheer, one/begun) gives it a chant-like quality — draw attention to this during choral reading so students hear the pattern before they analyse it. The comprehension questions in Let us Think A ask about teamwork and helping, which are anchored directly in the poem's first and second couplets, so refer students back to those lines when they respond.

periods.activity_title: Deeper Reading — Meaning, Mood and Rhyme

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.2): revisit and extend answers on teamwork with evidence from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Re-read the poem together once chorally (textbook pp.1–2), students tracking the text with a finger. This quick re-reading settles the language before the discussion begins.

Comprehension discussion: teacher poses open questions drawing on the poem's imagery — 'What picture comes to mind when you read "each hand joined"?' and 'Why does the poet say joy is born from a team, not from winning alone?' Students respond orally; teacher notes key ideas on the board.

Let us Think — A. (p.2): students write their answers to the two questions ('What happens when you join hands?' and 'Why is helping important?') in their notebooks, using evidence from the poem. Teacher circulates and prompts with line references.
Pair-share: students read their written answers to a partner and together decide which line from the poem best supports each answer. One or two pairs share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and chanted its rhymes together, students now bring those shared sounds into written comprehension — encourage them to quote a phrase rather than paraphrase. A common difficulty at this level is answering in isolated words; model a full-sentence response on the board using a phrase from the poem such as 'a bond of trust'.

periods.activity_title: Speaking Together — Discussion and Partner Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): discuss experiences of joy, teamwork, and losing a game.
Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.2): partner role-play — exchange favourite food and festival using sentence frame.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the discussion by recalling the poem's line 'Win or lose, we always share' and inviting students to think about a time they felt that spirit. This grounds the speaking tasks in the poem's theme of shared experience.

Let us Think + Let us Speak — B. (p.2): teacher leads a guided class discussion on the four oral prompts — feelings of joy, a cooperative activity with a friend, losing a game, and resolving a team disagreement. Students take turns responding; teacher models a full-sentence response for the first prompt to set expectations.

Partner role-play (p.2): students turn to the classmate beside them and exchange the Bokali–Darsana conversation, then each completes the sentence frame aloud ('My favourite food is ___. My favourite festival is ___.') Teacher circulates, listening and offering quiet prompts where needed.
Two or three pairs briefly share what they learnt about their partner's favourite festival. Teacher closes by connecting the idea of different traditions to the poem's image of 'hearts as one'.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's celebration of unity across difference ('different traditions, food, festivals, and languages') is the bridge between the Bokali–Darsana dialogue and the guided discussion questions — making this connection explicit helps students speak with genuine content rather than generic phrases. The fourth discussion question (resolving a team disagreement) is the most demanding; if time runs short, use it as a brief whole-class brainstorm rather than individual turns.

periods.activity_title: Collective Nouns — Groups That Go Together

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4): picture-based fill-in with collective nouns from the word box.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4): write two original sentences, each using a different collective noun from the unit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces collective nouns by connecting to the poem: 'The poem describes a team — what do we call a group of bees, or wolves?' Students guess freely; teacher lists suggestions on the board and introduces the term 'collective noun'.

Let us Learn — A. (pp.3–4): students look at the eight pictures in the textbook and, working individually, fill in the blanks using words from the box (choir, pack, grove, herd, swarm, bunch, bouquet). Teacher does the first example ('a bundle of sticks') aloud together, then students complete the rest.

Whole-class check: teacher calls on students to read each answer aloud. For any wrong answer, the class plays a quick 'category clue' game — teacher gives one defining clue about the group (e.g. 'they buzz and make honey') and students self-correct.

Rapid oral round: teacher says a collective noun from the set and students call out what group it names, then reverse — teacher names the group and students call out the collective noun. This consolidates the new vocabulary through playful repetition.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often confuse 'herd' and 'pack' — clarify that 'herd' is used for domestic or grazing animals (sheep, cattle) while 'pack' is associated with animals that hunt together (wolves). The pictures in the textbook (pp.3–4) are the primary scaffold, so ensure every student has the book open before beginning the fill-in.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions of Place — Where Things Are

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.5): map-based fill-in using prepositions of place (behind, between, near, in front of).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple sketch on the board — a school, a park, and a shop — and asks students to describe where each building is in relation to the others. This elicits the prepositions (near, behind, in front of, between) in natural speech before the textbook map is opened.

Let us Learn — B. (p.5): students open textbooks to the town map. Teacher names each location on the map (hospital, bank, post office, school, bookstore, children's park) and students point to each one. Students then complete the four fill-in blanks individually using the word box (behind, between, near, in front of).

Pair check: students compare answers with a partner and explain why each preposition fits ('The ambulance is between the post office and the hospital because it is in the middle'). Teacher circulates and hears two or three explanations.

Teacher asks two or three students to describe a different pair of places on the map using a preposition of their choice — for example, 'The school is _______ the bank.' This extends the grammar concept beyond the four set items.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with collective nouns as words for groups that belong together, students now move to prepositions — words that describe where things sit in relation to each other, another form of relational language. The map (p.5) is the key visual; ask students to trace the route between two buildings with a finger before writing, as physical orientation helps them select the correct preposition.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.6–7): observe five helping scenes and write short answers describing each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the five scenes on the board (or walks students through textbook pp.6–7) one by one, asking 'What do you see? Who is helping whom?' Students observe and respond orally before any writing begins. This picture-walk primes vocabulary — 'injured', 'crossing the road', 'art project'.

Modelled writing: teacher takes the first picture (Lubang and the injured friend) and thinks aloud while writing a model answer on the board — 'Lubang is supporting his injured friend. They will go to the school nurse together.' Students note the two-part pattern: what is happening now and what comes next.

Let us Write — A. (pp.6–7): students write answers for all five scenes in their notebooks, following the two-part pattern. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with a question: 'What are they doing right now?' and 'What do you think will happen next?'

Sharing round: four or five students read one of their answers aloud. Class listens for the two-part pattern (present action + next step) and gives a thumbs-up when they hear it. Teacher offers brief, specific praise or one gentle correction per response.

periods.teacher_notes: The five pictures in the textbook (pp.6–7) show different acts of helping — supporting an injured friend, cleaning a classroom, assisting an elderly person, a group art project, and students raising hands — all reflecting the poem's theme of people working together. Watch for students who write only the visible action without predicting the next step; the modelled example on the board gives them a sentence structure they can adapt for each picture.

periods.activity_title: Creating a Symbol of Togetherness — Paper-Chain Figures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Do You Know + Let us Do (pp.3–8): discuss honeybee waggle dance and ant teamwork, then create paper-chain figures.
Let us Do — A. (pp.7–8): fold, draw, cut, and colour paper-chain figures as a symbol of togetherness.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shares the Do You Know information (pp.3–8) about honeybees' waggle dance and ants' teamwork signals, asking students: 'How is what the bees do similar to what the poem describes about human teamwork?' Students make two or three connections aloud.

Teacher demonstrates the paper-chain figure steps on a fresh sheet — folding, drawing half a body outline, cutting, and unfolding — talking through each step so students can follow. Materials are distributed: plain paper, pencil, scissors, crayons.

Let us Do — A.: students work through all five steps independently — fold, draw, cut, unfold, and colour their paper-chain figures. Teacher circulates to support students with the folding and cutting, the two steps where fine-motor difficulty most often appears.

Gallery share: students hold up their completed figures and the class looks at the variety of designs. Teacher closes by connecting the unfolded chain back to the poem — 'When we unfolded the paper, what did we see? That is exactly what the last line says: together we shine, our hearts as one.'

periods.teacher_notes: The waggle-dance and ant-teamwork facts in the Do You Know section connect animal cooperation to the poem's theme of solidarity — this brief discussion is worth the minutes because it moves the concept beyond human social life. For the craft steps, pre-fold one demonstration sheet before the unit begins so the folding direction is clear when you show it; imprecise folding is the most common reason the chain separates when students cut.

items.source_context: Poem on teamwork and unity; end-rhyme pairs; imagery of joined hands and shared joy.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 1 beginning "Together we stand, strong and tall". According to these opening lines, what two things happen when the team stands together?

options.label: A
options.text: They become strong and never fall.

options.label: B
options.text: They win every game they play.

options.label: C
options.text: They share a prize with each other.

options.label: D
options.text: They shout and cheer the loudest.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Students who choose this may think the poem is about winning, missing its message that strength matters regardless of outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a conflation of the 'we always share' couplet with the opening lines about standing tall.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has substituted the cheering imagery from the second couplet into the first.

items.source_lo: Student locates evidence in a poem and constructs short answers using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem on teamwork and unity; end-rhyme pairs; imagery of joined hands and shared joy.
items.item_stem: The poem says "Win or lose, we always share, / Our bond of trust is always there." In one or two sentences, explain what the poet means by a "bond of trust" and why the team shares both winning and losing.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The "bond of trust" means the teammates rely on and believe in one another. The poet says they share both winning and losing because their friendship and support for each other matter more than the result.

items.source_lo: Student expresses personal experiences and ideas through guided and free conversation using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Guided discussion on joy, cooperative activities, losing gracefully, and resolving team conflict.
items.item_stem: The poem says "Cheering aloud, we shout and sing, / Teamwork can overcome anything." Decide whether each statement below is TRUE or FALSE.

options.text: According to the poem, a team that cheers together feels that working together helps them overcome challenges.
The poem suggests that only the loudest team members help the group succeed.
The poem shows that joy in a team comes from what everyone does together, not from a single person.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: the couplet directly states that teamwork overcomes anything, and cheering is the collective act that drives it. 2 — False: the poem never singles out any one member; the imagery throughout is of shared action (joined hands, collective cheering). 3 — True: the closing lines ('Together we shine, our hearts as one, / For in our team, the joy's begun') place joy in the collective effort.

items.item_stem: Think about a time you worked with friends on something — a game, a project, or any shared task. Tell your teacher: what did you do together, how did it feel, and what made working as a team better than working alone?

expected_elements: Names a specific shared activity clearly.
Describes a feeling using at least one word.
Explains one advantage of working together.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 6 showing Anna helping an old lady. Choose the sentence that best describes what Anna is doing and what the old lady will do next.

options.label: A
options.text: Anna is helping the old lady cross the road safely, and the old lady will reach her destination.

options.label: B
options.text: Anna is carrying the old lady's bag home, and the old lady will cook dinner.

options.label: C
options.text: Anna is teaching the old lady to read, and the old lady will write a letter.

options.label: D
options.text: Anna is waving goodbye to the old lady, and the old lady will go to the market.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have noticed Anna near the old lady but invented an action not visible in the picture.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student is associating helping with a school-related act rather than reading the picture carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have seen a gesture of acknowledgement and misread it as a farewell.

items.item_stem: Match each animal with the teamwork behaviour it uses.

Animal | Teamwork Behaviour
Honeybee | Performs a waggle dance to share the location of food
Ant | Uses signals to find food, defend the colony, and build nests

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Honeybee–Performs a waggle dance to share the location of food; Ant–Uses signals to find food, defend the colony, and build nests

answer_key.right: Performs a waggle dance to share the location of food
Uses signals to find food, defend the colony, and build nests
